title: What It Means to Be a Doctor
paragraphs: I did clerkships for a total of nine weeks in neurosurgery and plastic surgery at Johns Hopkins University in Baltimore, USA, and for three weeks in neurosurgery at Peking University in Beijing, China. Every clerkship was a very fulfilling time and a wonderful, irreplaceable experience.

Neurosurgery is divided into four teams: Brem, Cushing, Dandy and Pediatric. Johns Hopkins University is the birthplace of neurosurgery, and the teams are named like this, I am told, to honor the achievements of Drs. Cushing and Dandy, who founded neurosurgery there. I rotated through each team for one week.

The morning meeting time was 5 o'clock. I had heard rumors that surgical departments in America start early in the morning, but, to be honest, getting up at 4 was a battle with myself. When I arrived at the hospital, the residents had already checked the patients' charts, and I joined the residents' rounds from 5:30. Even though it was 5:30, it was pitch dark outside and most of the patients were still dreaming, but the residents mercilessly woke them up and began taking histories and doing neurological examinations. After that came a resident seminar from 6:30, the NCCU (Neurosciences Critical Care Unit) conference from 7:00, and surgical observation from 7:30, a very dense schedule. In surgery I basically served as an assistant, and depending on the resident I was allowed to irrigate and tie knots while looking through the microscope. Naturally, the doctors did not offer me procedures, and I could not do them unless I spoke up and said that I wanted to.

In America, the spine and peripheral nerves are also the responsibility of neurosurgery, so 5,000 operations a year are performed in two hospitals, and even at Johns Hopkins Hospital's neurosurgery alone, seven or more operating rooms were in full operation from 7 a.m. Operations ended at 17:00 to 19:00, and if I did not go home, eat and go straight to sleep, sufficient sleep was not guaranteed. So when an operation occasionally ended early, I felt happy just to be able to go home while it was still light, which was also an experience unique to America.

At the start of the clerkship, the residents and nurses did not pay much attention to me, perhaps because they were busy. So I actively greeted them with "How are you?", showed an attitude of helping even with small things, and tried to prove that I was a useful presence for them. Then everyone's attitude gradually changed, they began greeting me first, and I came to be allowed to help with ward procedures and preoperative preparations.

The types of surgery were wide-ranging, and there were five or more brain tumor operations a day. The brain tumor operations, decompression surgeries and so on were simply vast in number, and the surgeries themselves were not much different from Japan. What left an impression was that there were as many as three craniotomies for glioblastoma a day, which is very rare in Japan. I could also see minimally invasive spinal stabilisation using a robot, which has not yet been introduced in Japan. In an operation for a cerebellar tumor, however, I thought the wound was larger than in Japan, and when I talked about it with a neurosurgeon from neighboring China, that doctor had the same opinion. Perhaps Asians are better at delicate hand movements.

Even patients undergoing craniotomy came to the hospital on the morning of surgery, and the hospital stay was only two days. In America, which has no universal health insurance, it was common sense to shorten hospital stays. A doctor taught me, "A long hospital stay actually makes your condition worse." There were also allied health professionals not seen in Japan, with qualifications such as Physician Assistants, who handle ward management and miscellaneous work while the doctor operates, and Nurse Anesthetists, who take charge of the stable phase of anesthesia after the anesthesiologist has induced it, aiming at efficiency in medical care.

Sometimes I used my free time to ask the doctor in charge of consults and accompany him to see patients of other departments. In America there is no initial residency training, so after graduation you must immediately choose your own field. American interns differ depending on the specialty. Each department always has a resident in charge of consults, and a system was in place to consult immediately as soon as one strays even slightly from one's own specialty.

In the pediatric neurosurgery team, when I said I wanted to have a patient of my own, I was told to go and take the history and do the neurological examination of a patient who had had part of the brain removed. With no examination instruments at all, I tested tendon reflexes with my middle finger, pain and temperature sensation by pinching, and deep sensation using the vibration function of my iPhone, and I remember being very happy that I could identify the site of the sensory disturbance more accurately than I had expected.

One morning when I went to the hospital, a patient whose brain had been penetrated by a bullet had been admitted to my team. The patient in the NCCU had lost consciousness, had pinpoint pupils, and had barely been kept alive by a ventilator. When I asked the doctor, a brain death determination was planned once the body temperature recovered. I sincerely felt that I can never forgive a weapon that takes a precious life in an instant.

Plastic surgery is one of the most popular departments in America. This is because, owing to the health insurance system, it has top-level high income, it is also a gateway to cosmetic surgery, and the hospitals where one can train are very limited. Plastic surgery at Johns Hopkins University consists of three teams in total: the Hoopes and Edgerton teams at Johns Hopkins Hospital and a team at Johns Hopkins Bayview Hospital. The Hoopes team mainly handled breast reconstruction, microsurgical reconstruction and general reconstruction, the Edgerton team handled craniofacial, pediatric and gender-affirming surgery, and Bayview Hospital handled hand surgery and burns. I rotated with the Hoppes team for 2.5 weeks and with each of the remaining teams for one week.

The morning meeting time was 5:30, after the residents' merciless rounds, surgery started at 7:30, and with more than 13 hours of clerkship every day (the latest I experienced was 1:30 at midnight), it was a more intense schedule than neurosurgery. Plastic surgery at Johns Hopkins University was busier than is imaginable in Japan, with more than 20 operations a day and nearly 30 breast-related operations a week alone. A characteristic of plastic surgery was also that it treated students as a part of the team's workforce.

In surgery I imitated the Johns Hopkins students and, when I picked up the electrocautery on my own and cauterised bleeding sites, nothing was said to me. After that I proactively did hemostasis, irrigation and suction on my own. The wounds were often large, and when a doctor handed me a needle holder and forceps and said "Suture half of this," I felt half joy and half anxiety. During the one-month clerkship I was allowed to practise a great deal, from fat suturing to dermal suturing and subcutaneous suturing. (Practising knot tying and suturing little by little since I was a fourth-year student, during hospital visits and clerkships in surgery and obstetrics and gynecology, was very useful. I recommend that juniors who hope to enter surgical fields practise before studying abroad.) Also, besides scheduled operations, I was suddenly called in when another surgery's wound was too large or a flap was needed, so on many days operations were left on standby even late at night. One day I was in surgery past 21:00 when the cell phone in my breast pocket suddenly kept vibrating, and after a while the operating room nurses were buzzing about a shooting between the hospital and the dormitory. My blood ran cold, and I could not help worrying about how I would get back to the dormitory. Fortunately, that day too I got home safely by Johns Hopkins University's free ride service and was relieved. When I did my one-week clerkship at Johns Hopkins Bayview Hospital, the free shuttle bus ran only from 6:30 in the morning, so I chose the Baltimore city bus as my commuting method. In the dim early morning hours, I rode, fearfully, a bus where everyone was Black. On the last day I felt sick from an extremely strong smell of cannabis from the person next to me and the person behind. Baltimore's public safety is very bad. By exposing myself to a dangerous environment, I was able to realise anew how precious Japan's safe environment is.

At Bayview Hospital, by the chief's policy, students were required to check the charts of all patients, go on rounds alone and report the content to the residents. In fact, even on the fifth and final day I did not know what procedures I should do, so I could not achieve the goal of doing rounds alone. I felt frustrated, thinking that if I had been able to do a clerkship at this hospital for a longer period, I might have been able to manage patients by myself like the Johns Hopkins students. Also, at Bayview, besides entering the usual sterile field, I was allowed to write preoperative consent forms, hand over to the PACU (Pre and Post Anesthesia Care Unit) after surgery, and even do pre-visit history-taking in the outpatient clinic, and I was given the chance to look up papers and give a 20-minute presentation. One day an emergency gunshot operation came in and finished at midnight, so I stayed overnight at the hospital unplanned. There was no 24-hour convenience store as in Japan and going outside was dangerous, so getting food, water and bedding from those around me by myself and getting through the night was also an interesting experience.

In the last week, on a day when there were not enough residents, there was a skin graft operation on a leg in which I assisted as first assistant. It was my first time as first assistant, I approached the operation nervously, and fortunately I was not scolded by the doctor. While closing the wound, the attending said, "You helped me today, I'll leave the rest to you," suddenly took off his surgical gown and went somewhere. I looked around, but even the anesthesia was by a Nurse Anesthetist, and there was not a single doctor in the room. I calmed myself down, recalled my memories up to then and completed the suturing, wrapped three kinds of gauze, then took the patient to the ward and handed over to the nurse. When I later told a resident about this, he simply said "Good job." How much students are entrusted with seems to vary by department, but I think plastic surgery is without doubt the department that makes students the most Contributors to the team.

In plastic surgery I also experienced many cases not seen in Japan. They included the Charles Procedure for the most severe lymphedema (stripping the skin around the lower leg, cutting off the layer of fibrous tissue inside with scissors and laying the skin back), Le Fort III Osteotomy for a patient with Crouzon Syndrome (stripping the skin of the face from the scalp to below the eyes, cutting the cheekbone, pulling out the lower cheekbone and returning the skin), and for transgender patients Metoidioplasty (female-to-male gender-affirming surgery) and Penile Inversion Vaginoplasty (male-to-female gender-affirming surgery). Seeing them in person was a series of shocks, but these were also the moments when I really thought it was good to have come all the way to America for the clerkship.

In America, only high achievers can choose popular departments. This time I was able to do clerkships in neurosurgery and plastic surgery, which are extremely competitive in America. In clerkships in America, you can be idle as much as you like, and if you participate actively you can experience wonderful clerkships unimaginable in Japan. How fruitful you make your study abroad depends on yourself.

At Peking University, even before the clerkship, the administrative office replied quickly and I had the impression that they take very good care of people. Each exchange student had a supervising professor and a medical student mentor (I think it is the only one among Nagoya University's partner schools). The mentors mainly gave consultation and mediation on problems with study and life.

I did a three-week clerkship at Beijing Hospital, a community hospital. Beijing Hospital belongs to the "Grade 3A hospitals," the highest level in China's hospital ranking. The team led by Chief 王, a nationally famous neurosurgeon, was the first in China to introduce catheter techniques and is still at the top of the country in cerebrovascular treatment. In China the leading cause of death is cerebrovascular disease, and the team accepted patients referred from all over the country. I belonged to the vascular group and experienced many difficult endarterectomies, stent placements and aneurysm coil embolizations. The facilities and techniques were at a high level, almost the same as in Japan. In endarterectomies and so on, I was allowed to be second assistant and was also allowed to do subcutaneous and skin suturing.

The morning meeting time was 7:30, and I checked the condition of the patients operated on the previous day myself and took part in the morning handover from 8:00. All communication was in Chinese, but several doctors had done observerships at Johns Hopkins University in the US and the University of Chicago, and they explained medical terms to me in English. The English ability of the young doctors in master's and doctoral courses was also very high. The doctors were very enthusiastic about teaching, and when there was a procedure or an emergency, they even called me by phone to come, even if I was not there.

Because I can speak Chinese, I had many opportunities to talk with patients and their families during rounds. In the second week there was a patient in my charge with whom I had enjoyable conversations about trips to Japan and to whom I had become a little attached. However, that patient suddenly deteriorated late one night, and when I went to the hospital the next morning the patient had already passed away, which made me sad. Also, patients with subarachnoid hemorrhage were frequently brought to the emergency department, and when I explained the seriousness of the disease and the risks of treatment, I saw many families break down in tears. Faced directly with life and death, I could not help feeling the gravity of a doctor's responsibility and sometimes also powerlessness.

One day, while I was observing a carotid artery stenting, an embolus suddenly flew off and caused basilar artery occlusion. The atmosphere in the cath lab changed at once, but through the doctor's swift and calm manipulation the embolus was aspirated immediately. The chief said it was the first time in ten years, but I thought that since any kind of accident can happen in the clinical setting, doctors are required to have instant judgment at such times.

In most Chinese hospitals including Beijing Hospital, the doctors' office is inside the ward. Interestingly, when patients and their families had a question, they did not ask the nurses but visited the doctors' office directly. Although many patients may feel reassured by the closeness between doctors and patients, the doctors were forced to deal with patients coming in every five minutes even in the middle of their regular work. Even when the doctor was walking down the corridor or examining another patient, families stared from outside and threw various questions at the doctor the moment he left the patient's room. But the content of the questions was always light matters that could be solved by asking a nurse, such as why the MRI examination had not started yet or asking the doctor to look at a patient who said his back was itchy. Moreover, I also often saw people who, even though they had not had an outpatient visit or been admitted, were desperately waiting in the corridor to seek a second opinion with CT or MRI taken at another hospital. In addition, many patients called the doctors' mobile phones directly.

I was told that underlying such behavior, which is rarely seen in Japan, is a distrust of doctors that still remains: that doctors will not see you first unless you use connections or money, and that you cannot receive good medical care. Certainly for patients who have come to Beijing from far-off regions, considering lodging costs and so on, shortening the waiting time leads to reducing the financial burden.

Why do they have to come all the way to Beijing from the regions? Behind that is a social problem, the uneven distribution of China's medical resources. In "first-tier cities" such as Beijing and Shanghai, guidelines such as those of the WHO are actively adopted and exchange with foreign countries is lively, so one can receive medical care at the same level as in developed countries. In the regions, on the other hand, development has not yet reached them, and to receive good medical care one has to go to a big city. As a result, difficult cases gather in Beijing, the level of Beijing's doctors rises even higher, and regional gaps only widen.

Outside the clerkship, I could see a culture that values meals very much. Free lunch boxes were provided every day for each operating room, in the cath lab fruit was always prepared besides lunch, and when it was late at night they even treated me to dinner. During the three weeks of the clerkship at Beijing Hospital, I never once bought a meal with my own money. Instead of the Japanese "otsukaresama," I was always asked "Have you eaten?", and if I answered "No," the technicians and nurses prepared rice and plenty of side dishes along with fruit and sweets. Perhaps because I had just returned from America, which is indifferent to meals, I felt deeply the warmth and humanity of being at my parents' home.

Transportation such as buses and subways was very well developed, and shared bicycles were very cheap and easy to ride, so in terms of transportation I had the impression that it was more convenient than Nagoya. What surprised me on this trip to China was that smartphone payment had penetrated every corner of life. During the three weeks in China, I never used cash. Vending machines where you can pay with your face and barcodes posted everywhere in the hospital stood out, and even to a white-haired elderly street musician I had to give money by barcode. We can expect further development of healthcare and social welfare in this country, which has achieved rapid economic growth.

Whatever field a doctor goes into in the future, in order to acquire the latest information they must read papers and attend academic conferences. Unfortunately, the official language of medicine is likely to remain English both now and in the near future. Reading papers and giving conference presentations in English themselves should be easy by looking things up in smartphone dictionaries and Google. However, because medicine is advancing day by day in the information society, the ability to discuss in English with doctors all over the world is now required. Looking at history too, a country that refuses exchange gets left behind in the world's rally.

I think that a doctor should stay abroad, even for a short period, for clinical work or research. It does not have to be an English-speaking country. This is because the moment you leave Japan the other party cannot speak Japanese, so the tool of exchange ends up being English. The other party's English is not necessarily high either. I think true English ability is being able to communicate smoothly even with simple words and grammar. Honestly, one cannot expect an improvement in English ability from an exchange study abroad either, but I believe that the ability to make skilful use of one's limited vocabulary and to discuss and negotiate with people from abroad grows without one noticing.

Of course, Japanese medicine also leads the world, always incorporates the latest knowledge and techniques, and people's morals are the highest in the world. Working as a doctor in Japan is a wonderful choice. That is exactly why I want even juniors who plan to work in Japan in the future not to miss the wonderful chance of Nagoya University's exchange study abroad, which allows them to stay abroad and grow. Finally, I would like to offer my greatest thanks to Dr. 長谷川, Dr. 粕谷, Dr. Itzel and the staff of the International Collaboration Office who supported this study abroad, one of the greatest events of my life, to the professors of the host universities, Johns Hopkins University and Peking University, and to my parents.
